strengths: The paper identifies a useful problem: explanations based on interpretable concepts can suffer from unmeasured confounding even when predictions are deterministic functions of pixels. This distinction should interest researchers in interpretability, causal discovery, and model auditing.

Using FCI and PAGs provides an established foundation for representing causal ambiguity under latent confounding. The background constraint that predictions cannot cause image contents is well motivated.

The presentation explains the conceptual motivation clearly, supplies a concrete simulation, and explores two application domains. The discussion acknowledges partial identification and the importance of expert-selected features. Applying existing methods to this explanation problem is a legitimate contribution without requiring a new algorithm.
weaknesses: Necessary—calibrate the causal conclusions. Section VI combines directed and circle-arrow edges into one stability score, although a circle-arrow edge can represent entirely confounded association. Bootstrap stability therefore does not establish causal influence. Likewise, absence of adjacency to the prediction does not exclude an indirect causal effect through other features. Statements identifying features as important determinants or causally irrelevant exceed these results. Report definite and ambiguous relationships separately and restrict conclusions to what the estimated equivalence classes support.

Necessary—repair the Shapley example. In the appendix, the calculation with Z3 omitted still evaluates the prediction function at a fixed, unobserved z3 and changes from a three-player to a two-player game. This is not a derivation of the stated backdoor adjustment using observed Z2 alone. Moreover, the purported causal coalition values do not generally propagate interventions through descendants in the supplied SCM. Define the intervention and value function precisely, then provide a valid comparison that isolates the effect of missing confounders.

Necessary—establish the simulation's causal ground truth. Inspecting logistic-regression coefficients on learned shape predictions does not establish that the complete image-to-prediction pipeline depends only on the true V and H variables. Other shapes could affect the learned detectors, whose accuracy is imperfect. Report the coefficients and verify the claimed invariance through controlled image interventions, or construct a predictor whose dependence on the intended shapes is guaranteed.

Necessary—address selection in the X-ray experiment. Controls are selected to have no reported findings, while pneumonia cases may contain the explanatory findings. This sampling can induce dependencies through selection, which is distinct from marginalizing latent confounders. The manuscript dismisses selection bias as irrelevant without justifying that assumption here. Account for the sampling mechanism or narrow this experiment to exploratory associations; clinical plausibility alone does not validate the inferred causes of model predictions.

Necessary—support the conditional-independence testing. Pearson chi-square tests involving multivalued bird attributes, nine prediction classes, and up to four conditioning variables can produce very sparse contingency tables. The 239-image X-ray analysis also raises sparse-cell concerns. No diagnostics establish adequate test calibration. Bootstrap repetition cannot correct systematically unreliable tests. Provide relevant diagnostics and sensitivity analyses, or temper the empirical causal claims accordingly.

Necessary—resolve reporting inconsistencies. The stated bird splits sum to 3,898 images, exceeding the reported total of 3,538. The X-ray accuracy of 74.55% is unexplained for a 50-image test set. Figure 9 calls Wing Shape and Wing Pattern the most stable causes, whereas Figure 8 ranks Size, Eye Color, and Bill Shape highest and places Wing Shape near the bottom. Explain whether different statistics are intended and specify which observations were used for graph discovery.

Optional—strengthen the comparative evaluation. The LIME/SHAP examples illustrate differences in explanatory granularity, but do not establish superior causal accuracy. Comparisons using the same concept annotations, and repeated simulations measuring causal classification errors, would better isolate the benefit of causal discovery.
